role: Nursemaid and servant of the Prophet ﷺ from his infancy
One of the survivors of the earliest generation
summary: Umm Ayman (RA), whose real name was Barakah al-Habashiyyah, was an Abyssinian slave woman who served in the household of Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's father, before the Prophet ﷺ was born. She nursed and cared for the Prophet ﷺ from infancy, outlived him by a few months, and was called by him 'my mother after my mother.' She is one of the most intimate figures of the Prophetic household.
biography:
Barakah bint Tha'labah, known universally as Umm Ayman, was an Abyssinian slave woman who belonged to the household of Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib — the Prophet's father. She was already in the household when the Prophet ﷺ was born around 570 CE, and after the death of his mother Aminah bint Wahb (which occurred when the Prophet ﷺ was approximately six years old), she became his primary caretaker along with his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib, and then after his grandfather's death, his uncle Abu Talib.

The Prophet ﷺ inherited Umm Ayman from his father's estate as a young man, but before his marriage to Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, he freed her. Even after her freedom, she chose to remain associated with his household out of deep attachment. Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra and al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' record that the Prophet ﷺ said of her: 'Umm Ayman is my mother after my mother (ummi ba'da ummi).' This single statement from the Prophet ﷺ establishes her unique and irreplaceable place in the Seerah.

After being freed, she was married first to Ubayd ibn Zayd al-Khazraji of Madinah, with whom she had a son named Ayman ibn Ubayd. Ayman accepted Islam and died as a martyr at the Battle of Hunayn (8 AH), fighting beside the Prophet ﷺ. After Ubayd's death, the Prophet ﷺ asked who among the Sahaba would marry 'a woman of the people of Paradise,' and Zayd ibn Harithah (RA) — the Prophet's freed slave and beloved companion — stepped forward and married her. Their son was Usamah ibn Zayd (RA), the Beloved of the Messenger. Umm Ayman thus became the mother of two martyrs of different generations: Ayman at Hunayn, and Usamah's father Zayd at Mu'tah.

She accepted Islam at the very beginning of the prophetic mission, among the first group to believe. Her Islam was never in doubt — it preceded the formal declaration of the religion in many ways, as she had lived with the Prophet ﷺ from his infancy. Al-Dhahabi notes she is counted among the earliest Muslims.

A well-known account preserved in Sirah sources and authenticated narrations describes how, during the Hijrah, Umm Ayman made the journey from Makkah to Madinah on foot and alone — a journey across harsh terrain of hundreds of miles. She reportedly became desperately thirsty and was near death when she found water. Another account records that she made a portion of the journey fasting and found water miraculously at the point of collapse. Ibn Sa'd records these reports in al-Tabaqat. Whatever the exact details, the classical sources unanimously describe the Hijrah as a profound test of her devotion.

She was present in Madinah throughout the Prophetic period and witnessed nearly every major event. When the Prophet ﷺ died in 11 AH (632 CE), the Sahaba were overwhelmed with grief. Abu Bakr and Umar visited Umm Ayman to pay their respects, and they found her weeping. When asked why she wept — since she knew the Prophet ﷺ was now with Allah — she replied: 'I knew already that the Messenger of Allah would die, but I weep because revelation (wahy) has ceased from the heavens.' This answer, recorded in Sahih Muslim and other sources, moved Abu Bakr and Umar to tears as well.

She died in 20 AH (641 CE), a few months after the death of Umar ibn al-Khattab, in Madinah, at an age likely around eighty. She was among the last surviving companions who had known the Prophet ﷺ from before his birth, and her passing marked the end of a living link to the very earliest era of his life.

key_events.event: Present as a slave in the household of Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib at the Prophet's birth
Became primary caretaker of the Prophet ﷺ after his mother Aminah's death
Freed by the Prophet ﷺ before his marriage to Khadijah
Accepted Islam among the earliest believers
Made the Hijrah from Makkah to Madinah, reportedly on foot
Her son Ayman ibn Ubayd was martyred at the Battle of Hunayn
Wept at the Prophet's death; told Abu Bakr and Umar she wept for the ending of revelation

notable_traits: Called 'my mother after my mother' by the Prophet ﷺ — among the most intimate of all relationships in the Seerah
One of the very few people who knew the Prophet ﷺ from before his prophetic mission and before his birth
Her weeping at the Prophet's death was for the end of revelation — a profoundly theological response
Made the Hijrah alone on foot — a feat of extraordinary devotion and endurance
